message:
Please review the following document.

Here is how its author describes it:

<author>
This proposal is built on our own trading history, not just competitor benchmarking, and that is what makes me confident in it. The key question with any rate rise is price sensitivity, and we have a direct test: when we raised the weekend rate by £10 last June, weekend occupancy went up, from 81% to 89%, the following month. Combined with a value-for-money score of 8.4, the best in our set, and rates £20 to £35 below competitors, everything points the same way. The revenue estimate is deliberately conservative: it assumes no occupancy gain and puts no value at all on the extra Friday and Sunday nights that the two-night minimum will generate, so £204,000 is a floor rather than a target. We have also built in a clear monitoring trigger, so if occupancy does dip we will see it within a month and can respond. Corporate and group commitments are protected. I think this is a well-evidenced, low-risk change that brings our pricing into line with the quality of the hotel.
</author>

The review is to check that the recommendation is clear and the document is ready to go to the decision-makers.

<document>
Pricing Proposal: Weekend Rate Restructure
Harbourside Hotel, Revenue Management, April 2026

1. Proposal
From 1 June 2026 we propose to (a) raise the Best Available Rate (BAR) for Friday and Saturday nights from £145 to £165, and (b) introduce a two-night minimum for any stay that includes a Saturday night. Midweek rates are unchanged.

2. Context
Harbourside is a 112-room four-star hotel on the quay, with a leisure-led weekend business and a corporate-led midweek business. Our weekend BAR is £20 to £35 below the three comparable hotels in our competitive set, whose weekend rates currently range from £165 to £180. Weekend occupancy has recovered strongly since 2023 and we believe we are leaving money on the table.

Table 1. Weekend (Friday and Saturday) occupancy by month, 2025
Jan 62% | Feb 66% | Mar 74% | Apr 80% | May 85% | Jun 81%
Jul 89% | Aug 93% | Sep 88% | Oct 82% | Nov 72% | Dec 78%

Average weekend occupancy across 2025 was 79%. July and August are our strongest months, driven by the harbour festival and the school summer holidays, with September also benefiting from late-season visitors.

3. Evidence on price sensitivity
In the last week of June 2025 we raised the weekend BAR by £10, from £135 to the current £145. Weekend occupancy in July rose to 89%, from 81% in June. This tells us that our weekend guests are not price sensitive at current levels; if anything, the higher rate appears to have reinforced our positioning as a quality option, and we expect the further increase to be absorbed in the same way.

This is consistent with feedback from our guest satisfaction surveys, where weekend guests rate "value for money" at 8.4 out of 10, the highest score among our competitive set.

4. Two-night minimum
Saturday nights are our most constrained inventory: we sold out on 31 Saturdays in 2025. Many of these guests stay only one night, leaving rooms empty on Friday or Sunday either side. A two-night minimum for stays including a Saturday will convert single-night Saturday stays into two-night stays and smooth occupancy across the weekend.

Our booking data show that weddings at Quayside Hall, the venue next door, account for around 38% of our Saturday-night room bookings. Wedding guests typically book as a block through the couple, arrive on the Saturday afternoon and check out on the Sunday morning.

5. Revenue impact
Across our 124 rooms, 104 weekend nights a year and average weekend occupancy of 79%, a £20 increase in BAR is worth about £204,000 a year in additional room revenue, before any gain from longer stays. We have assumed weekend occupancy is maintained at 2025 levels, which we consider prudent given the evidence above.

The two-night minimum should add further revenue through additional Friday and Sunday nights. We have not quantified this but expect it to be material, particularly in shoulder months.

6. Implementation and monitoring
The new rates will be loaded into the channel manager on 15 May for stays from 1 June, giving online travel agencies two weeks' notice. Corporate contracted rates and group rates already contracted will be honoured. We will review pick-up weekly against the same weeks in 2025 and report to the General Manager monthly. If weekend occupancy for any month falls more than five points below 2025, we will review the rate.

7. Recommendation
The evidence shows that our weekend guests are not price sensitive at current rates and that we are priced well below our competitive set. We recommend approval of the £165 weekend BAR and the two-night Saturday minimum from 1 June 2026, delivering at least £204,000 of additional annual room revenue.
</document>
response:
# Review: Weekend Rate Restructure Proposal

**The recommendation is clear, but the document is not ready for decision-makers.** The two claims the author relies on most, that the June 2025 rate rise proves guests aren't price sensitive and that £204,000 is a floor, are both contradicted by the document's own data.

## Major issues

### 1. The price-sensitivity evidence is confounded by seasonality
Section 3 attributes the July occupancy rise (81% → 89%) to the £10 rate increase. But Section 2 says July and August are the strongest months "driven by the harbour festival and the school summer holidays." Table 1 shows occupancy climbing to 93% in August and falling back to 88% in September, which is a seasonal pattern. A June-to-July rise is what you'd expect in any year, with or without a price change.

There's also a timing problem. The rise took effect in the last week of June, so most of June's 81% was achieved at the old rate.

What would make this evidence usable:
- Compare July–December 2025 against the same months in 2024. Those are like-for-like seasons at different prices.
- Show competitors' rate movements over the same period.
- Show booking pace or conversion from the rate-shopping/booking engine, rather than realised occupancy alone.

As written, Section 3 doesn't support "our weekend guests are not price sensitive." The recommendation in Section 7 rests on that claim.

### 2. The value-for-money score doesn't show the higher rate will hold
The 8.4 score was measured at £135–£145. It shows guests think the *current* price is good value. It doesn't show they'll feel the same at £165, where you'd be priced level with the cheapest competitor rather than below it. Some of that score may exist *because* you're cheaper.

### 3. Room count is inconsistent, and the revenue figure uses the wrong one
- Section 2: **112 rooms**.
- Section 5: **124 rooms**.

The £204,000 figure uses 124: 124 × 104 × 79% × £20 ≈ £203,800.
With 112 rooms the same calculation gives **≈ £184,000**. That's a £20,000 overstatement, if 112 is the correct count.

### 4. The £20 uplift is applied to rooms that won't pay BAR
The calculation assumes every occupied weekend room pays the £20 increase. But:
- Section 6 says corporate and contracted group rates will be honoured.
- Section 4 says wedding guests make up **~38% of Saturday bookings** and book as blocks through the couple. These are almost certainly group or negotiated rates, not BAR.

So a large share of weekend room-nights won't see the increase. The true uplift is well below £204,000, probably below £184,000. **The "floor" is actually a ceiling.** Section 7's "delivering *at least* £204,000" should not go to decision-makers in its current form.

### 5. The two-night minimum may reduce occupancy, not just fail to add revenue
The author calls the estimate conservative because it assigns no value to the minimum stay. But the minimum stay carries a downside risk that the document doesn't address:
- **Weddings.** The document's own description says wedding guests arrive Saturday and leave Sunday. That is a one-night stay. Either weddings are exempt, which removes a large chunk of the claimed benefit, or wedding parties are pushed toward other hotels. The document needs to say which.
- **Displacement.** On the 31 sell-out Saturdays, the minimum may convert some one-night guests to two nights. Others will book elsewhere, and their Saturday may not be resold. On non-sell-out Saturdays, a minimum stay usually just turns away business.
- **Interaction with the rate rise.** Introducing both changes at once means a two-night weekend costs £40 more *and* requires a commitment some guests don't want.

"Assumes occupancy is maintained at 2025 levels" is therefore an assumption, not a prudent one. A sensitivity case would help, for example the revenue impact if occupancy falls 3, 5 or 8 points. For reference, the break-even occupancy loss on the BAR element alone is about 12% in relative terms (£20/£165), i.e. roughly 79% → 69%.

### 6. The dates appear to be out of date
The document is dated April 2026 and proposes implementation from 1 June 2026, with rates loaded on 15 May. It's now November 2026. If this hasn't been implemented:
- The dates need updating.
- Table 1 and the analysis should use 2026 trading data, which is now available, instead of 2025.

If it *has* been implemented, the document should report results rather than projections.

## Smaller points

- **Monitoring trigger.** A monthly comparison against 2025 will blend the effects of the rate rise and the minimum stay. It won't tell you which change caused a dip. Consider tracking Friday, Saturday and Sunday separately, plus denials or lost-business data for minimum-stay rejections. Also state what "review the rate" means: who decides, and what the options are.
- **First-year revenue.** Bookings already on the books for June onward at £145 will dilute year-one gains. Worth a sentence.
- **Competitive position.** At £165 you match the cheapest competitor. The document should say whether that's the intended positioning and how competitors are expected to respond.
- **"Leaving money on the table"** (Section 2) is asserted rather than shown. Issues 1–4 are what would show it.

## Suggested fixes before circulation

1. Confirm the room count and recompute revenue using only the BAR-paying share of weekend room-nights.
2. Replace the June-to-July comparison with a year-on-year comparison.
3. State how weddings and other groups are treated under the two-night minimum, and quantify the displacement risk.
4. Add a downside scenario table.
5. Change "at least £204,000" to an estimate with a range.
6. Update dates and data to the current trading year.

The underlying case may well be sound: being £20–£35 below the competitive set with strong satisfaction scores is a reasonable starting point. But the document currently presents a stronger and lower-risk case than its evidence supports. Decision-makers who spot the seasonality issue or the room-count discrepancy will likely question the rest.
